source.citation: 101 Last Tribes, Baka people, Global Bush Tour, Congo Basin Institute, and a Smithsonian Folkways review. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.home: The rainforests of southeast Cameroon, in the South and East regions, and neighbouring Congo, the Central African Republic and Gabon.
attributes.size: Estimates for Cameroon range from about 30,000 to about 40,000.
attributes.way_of_life: Traditionally hunter-gatherers. During the twentieth century many began to settle and adopt agriculture.
attributes.neighbours: They live alongside farming peoples such as the Njem.
attributes.spirituality: The Baka honour the forest spirit Jengi (also written Djengui or Ejengi).
attributes.knowledge: A deep knowledge of the forest, including the wild yam, which holds a central place in their cosmology between humans, elephants and forest spirits.
attributes.terminology: The outsider term pygmy is criticised for suggesting primitiveness, so use Baka or the group's own name.

source.citation: Smithsonian Folkways, Cameroon: Baka Pygmy Music, Susanne Fürniss in the African Music journal, and 101 Last Tribes. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.description: Vocal choirs in which several melodies are sung at the same time, with polyrhythmic percussion.
attributes.roles: The singing is done by women, while the men march the song, meaning they dance.
attributes.instruments: Baka music is essentially vocal, and instruments accompany the singing.
attributes.meaning: Singing and dancing are linked to the forest spirits and the ancestors.
attributes.recording: Smithsonian Folkways reissued the album Cameroon: Baka Pygmy Music in its UNESCO Collection of Traditional Music.
attributes.caution: One website says Baka polyphony is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. That listing refers to the Aka people of the Central African Republic and Congo, so it is not recorded here for the Baka.

source.citation: Wikipedia, Music of Cameroon (CC BY-SA 4.0). Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.description: A double-sided harp with calabash amplification, used by Beti storytellers.
attributes.role: The storytellers are viewed as using the mvet as an instrument of God to educate the people.
attributes.setting: Played at Beti gatherings such as parties, funerals and weddings.

source.citation: Wikipedia, Music of Cameroon (CC BY-SA 4.0). Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

content.name: Ekang and bikutsi phases of Beti gatherings

attributes.ekang_phase: The time when imaginary, mythological and spiritual issues are discussed. It is intensely musical, usually lasts all night, and has poetic recitations with clapping and dancing.
attributes.balafon: Interludes of improvised, sometimes obscene balafon playing signal the shift to the bikutsi phase.
attributes.bikutsi_phase: Much less strictly structured. Women dance and sing along with the balafon, and the lyrics deal with real-life problems.
attributes.rhythm: Bikutsi is characterised by an intense 6/8 rhythm.
attributes.balafon_orchestras: Balafon orchestras of three to five balafons with percussion became common in bars.
